variants.name: const-correct value semantics
variants.idiom_name: const member functions + constexpr + value semantics (std::span/std::string_view borrows)
variants.implementation_notes: C++ expresses immutability through qualifiers and value semantics rather than an Immutable class: const member functions make a state change impossible through a const reference, constexpr forces computation to compile time, and std::vector, std::string and std::array are values, so a copy is an independent version while std::span<const T> and std::string_view are the read-only borrow. What replaces the classic immutable structure is therefore the type system: mark every query const, return new values from update functions, and share snapshots as std::shared_ptr<const T>. The classic hand-written immutable class is still justified when the object must hide a large mutable representation behind a stable handle. Escape hatches - mutable members, const_cast, a const member function that returns a non-const pointer into the state - void the guarantee, and const alone does not make sharing thread-safe.
pitfalls: mutable data members and const_cast let code write through an otherwise const object, and a const member function returning a pointer or reference into the state hands that escape to callers.
const is shallow for pointees and smart pointers: const std::shared_ptr<T> protects the pointer, not the T it owns - write std::shared_ptr<const T>.
Returning a const reference to a member of a temporary dangles, so chained calls like cfg.with_port(1).name() must not outlive the temporary.

variants.name: immutable snapshots in std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<const T>>
variants.implementation_notes: Where several threads read configuration or routing data, the pattern becomes an atomically published immutable snapshot: the C++20 std::atomic<std::shared_ptr> specialization (and its weak_ptr companion) lets a writer exchange a whole const snapshot while readers load a reference to theirs and keep it stable for the duration of a request. Readers never lock, and no reader can see the writer's half-built version because the new value is constructed before the store. Prefer this over a mutex when reads dominate; prefer a plain shared_ptr<const T> plus a mutex when the C++20 atomic specialization is unavailable.
pitfalls: Readers must keep the shared_ptr alive for as long as they use the snapshot; a reference or raw pointer taken from a temporary shared_ptr dangles once the temporary dies.
std::atomic<std::shared_ptr> is C++20; on earlier standards use the free std::atomic_load/atomic_store functions with a plain shared_ptr, or a mutex.
Do not mutate the object a published snapshot points to - store a new const snapshot instead, or the guarantee breaks for every reader.
